## Subject-level drift rates and thresholds

To visualize the individual variability of our parameters of interest, distributions of the means of the subject-level posterior distributions for threshold (Learned and Novel) and drift rate (Learned and novel) can be found in @fig-ind-param.











::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Distribution of subject-level posterior means of the threshold parameter (Learned and Novel) and the drift rate parameter (Learned and Novel). Black doted lines denotate the median parameter estimates and the small color lines denotate the individual subject mean parameter estimates.](supplementary_files/figure-pdf/fig-ind-param-1.png){#fig-ind-param}
:::
:::


To assess whether participants' parameter estimates varied enough to support an individual-differences approach, we compared the spread of the subject-level posterior means with the precision of each individual estimate. Estimates from hierarchical models are shrunk toward the group mean, so their observed spread understates true between-participant variance. More importantly, variability is only meaningful when it exceeds the uncertainty of each estimate (Hedge et al., 2018; Rouder & Haaf, 2019; Haines et al., 2020). For each parameter and condition, we therefore computed the ratio of the between-participant SD of posterior means to the average within-participant posterior SD. Ratios were [1.88–2.04] for threshold and [1.307–1.535] for drift rate, indicating that participants differed by more than the uncertainty in their individual estimates. As a complementary check, we computed, for each participant, the 95% credible interval of their deviation from the group-level estimate. For threshold, 28.3% (learned) and 29.7% (novel) of participants deviated credibly from the group mean; for drift rate, the proportions were 11.0% (learned) and 18.3% (novel). All proportions exceed the maximum of 5% expected if participants did not differ, which is a conservative benchmark given hierarchical shrinkage. Together, these results indicate substantial between-participant variability.

## Bayesian linear regression models: Car predictor

As an exploratory analysis, we were interested to see how does object recognition ability predict the drift rate and threshold values from the face recognition task. 
We ran two Bayesian linear regression models: the first one to estimate if object recognition ability could predict the response caution for learned and novel response and the second one to estimate if object recognition ability could predict the different drift rates (TRUE, FALSE and TRUE-FALSE) for learned and novel face stimuli. The models specificity can be found in @tbl-regression-model-formula-car. 

{{< pagebreak >}}

*Threshold*: Regarding the threshold (response caution) predictions, visual inspections of the predictions show that as car recognition ability increases, the response caution for both, the Learned and Novel responses, increases (@fig-prediction-thresh-car).




::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Predicted threshold values from car recognition ability scores for learned and novel responses](supplementary_files/figure-pdf/fig-prediction-thresh-car-1.png){#fig-prediction-thresh-car}
:::
:::




*Drift rate (TRUE and FALSE)*: Regarding the drift rate (TRUE) and (FALSE), visual inspections of the predictions show that, as car recognition ability increases, both drift rate (TRUE and FALSE) for both stimuli conditions (Learned and Novel) increases as well. In summary, as car recognition ability increases, the accumulation of signal (drift rate TRUE) and the accumulation of noise (FALSE) increase, regardless of the stimulus condition (@fig-prediction-drift-car). 




::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Predicted drfit rate (TRUE and FALSE) values from car recognition ability scores for learned and novel faces](supplementary_files/figure-pdf/fig-prediction-drift-car-1.png){#fig-prediction-drift-car}
:::
:::




*Drift rate (TRUE-FALSE)*: Regarding the drift rate (TRUE-FALSE), or the signal-to-noise ratio provided by the stimulus, visual inspections of the predictions show that, as car recognition ability increases, only the drift rate for Novel faces increases, whereas the drift rate for Learned face does not follow this pattern. In summary, as car recognition ability increases, the ability to discriminate Novel faces increases but not the ability to discriminate Learned faces (@fig-prediction-drift-constrast-car).




::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Predicted drift rate (TRUE-FALSE) values from car recognition ability for learned and novel faces](supplementary_files/figure-pdf/fig-prediction-drift-constrast-car-1.png){#fig-prediction-drift-constrast-car}
:::
:::
